title: DNA Hairpin Treatment Cuts Bad Cholesterol Nearly 50% Without Statins
excerpt: Scientists in Spain and the United States built short DNA molecules that switch off a cholesterol-regulating gene, cutting blood cholesterol 47% in mice after a single injection — with none of the side effects linked to statins.
body:
• Researchers used DNA-based molecules called polypurine hairpins (PPRHs) to block production of PCSK9, a protein that limits the body's ability to clear "bad" LDL cholesterol.
  • A single injection of the lead molecule, HpE12, reduced cholesterol levels 47% in mice carrying the human PCSK9 gene by day three, and cut PCSK9 RNA in lab-grown liver cells by 74%.
  • The approach may avoid the muscle pain associated with statins, and is cheaper and more stable to manufacture than existing PCSK9 drugs such as inclisiran, evolocumab, and alirocumab.
  • The work is preclinical — tested in liver cells and mice, not yet in humans — so larger safety trials remain ahead before any clinical use.

A new DNA-based treatment has cut "bad" cholesterol levels by nearly half in animal testing, offering a potential alternative to statins for the millions of people who cannot tolerate the widely used drugs. The research, led by teams at the University of Barcelona and the University of Oregon, targets a protein called PCSK9 that regulates how the body clears cholesterol from the blood. Their findings were published in the journal Biochemical Pharmacology.

Instead of relying on a daily pill, the team designed short, folded strands of DNA known as polypurine hairpins (PPRHs) that bind directly to the PCSK9 gene and shut down its activity. When PCSK9 production is blocked, liver cells display more LDL receptors on their surfaces, pulling more low-density lipoprotein cholesterol — the "bad" kind linked to heart disease — out of circulation and into cells where it can be processed.

Context & Background

PCSK9 has become one of the most important targets in cardiovascular medicine over the past decade. The protein attaches to LDL receptors on cells and marks them for destruction. When PCSK9 levels are high, fewer receptors survive, and LDL cholesterol accumulates in the bloodstream, accelerating the fatty plaque buildup in artery walls known as atherosclerosis.

Several PCSK9-blocking medicines already exist. Monoclonal antibodies such as evolocumab and alirocumab, and the gene-silencing injection inclisiran, are prescribed to patients whose cholesterol resists statins. But these treatments are expensive, require repeated administration, and some can raise circulating PCSK9 levels as a side effect. Statins themselves, while effective and cheap, cause muscle pain and other adverse effects in a significant share of patients — one reason researchers keep hunting for alternatives.

The new study describes for the first time how two specific polypurine hairpins — dubbed HpE9 and HpE12 — reduce both PCSK9 RNA and protein while boosting LDL receptor levels. One arm of each hairpin chain binds precisely to polypyrimidine sequences in exons 9 and 12 of the PCSK9 gene, respectively, using Watson-Crick base pairing. That binding blocks the gene from being transcribed, interfering with the RNA polymerase machinery that would otherwise produce the protein.

Impact & Analysis

The numbers reported by the researchers are striking. In HepG2 liver cells, HpE12 decreased PCSK9 RNA levels by 74% and protein levels by 87%. In transgenic mice carrying the human PCSK9 gene, a single injection of HpE12 cut plasma PCSK9 levels 50% and cholesterol levels 47% by the third day.

"The results show that both HpE9 and HpE12 are highly effective in HepG2 cells. HpE12 decreases PCSK9 RNA levels by 74% and protein levels by 87%. In the case of transgenic mice, a single injection of HpE12 reduces plasma PCSK9 levels by 50% and cholesterol levels by 47% on the third day."

— Prof. Verònica Noé, University of Barcelona

According to the study's authors, polypurine hairpins carry practical advantages over other genetic medicines: they are inexpensive to synthesize, chemically stable, and do not trigger immune responses. "PPRHs, especially HpE12, are therapeutic oligonucleotides with many advantages, including low cost of synthesis, stability and lack of immunogenicity," the researchers concluded. They added that such an approach "would not lead to side effects such as the myopathies associated with statin therapy."

The caveat is real and the team acknowledges it. These are cell and mouse results, and therapies that lower cholesterol in mice frequently fail or need redesign before reaching patients. This is the first report of PPRH molecules being used against a metabolic condition like hypercholesterolemia, and the path from a promising injection in transgenic mice to a human drug involves years of toxicology work and clinical trials.

Diaspora Angle

The finding lands with particular weight for South Asians, who face some of the world's highest rates of premature heart disease and often develop cardiovascular problems at younger ages and lower cholesterol thresholds than other populations. Statins remain the standard defense, but tolerance issues push many patients to discontinue them. A cheaper, injectable, non-statin option — if it survives clinical testing — could eventually matter most in communities where statin use is already high and side effects are a common reason people stop taking their medication.

What's Next

The Barcelona and Oregon teams now need to test the therapy in larger animal models and complete detailed safety studies before human trials can be considered. The work was funded by Spain's Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities and the U.S. National Institutes of Health. If confirmed in further studies, the researchers say, the approach could become a safer, more targeted way to lower cholesterol — though no human timeline has been announced.
